text: Ken Noda, born October 5, 1962, is an American concert pianist, accompanist, vocal coach, and composer. He began composing music and performing as a concert pianist before the age of 11. He has performed with symphony orchestras worldwide and has composed numerous art songs and five operas. He worked as a vocal coach at the Metropolitan Opera from 1991 until retiring from his full-time position in July 2019. Born to Japanese parents in Dobbs Ferry, New York, Noda grew up in Scarborough and was educated at the Hackley School, graduating in 1980. He began studying the piano at age five and was admitted to the Juilliard School on a full scholarship at age seven. He studied piano privately with Daniel Barenboim, Adele Marcus, and Sylvia Rabinof and studied singing with Beverley Peck Johnson, serving as her studio accompanist at Juilliard for many years. In 1986, he received an Avery Fisher Career Grant worth $10,000 (equivalent to $28,685 in 2024). Noda composed his first opera, *The Canary and the Baseball*, at age 10, which premiered at the Brevard Music Festival on August 18, 1973, and was later staged by the educational wing of the New York City Opera. At age 13, he received a National Endowment for the Arts grant to compose a three-act opera, *The Rivalry* (1976), his third opera. He composed two additional operas: *The Highwayman* (1979) and *The Magic Turtle* (1980). By age 16, he had composed 65 art songs. Noda began performing early, and by age 14, he had appeared as a soloist with the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra, the Minnesota Orchestra, the St. Louis Symphony, and the New York Philharmonic. He has also performed with the Berlin Philharmonic, the Boston Symphony Orchestra, the Chicago Symphony, the Cleveland Orchestra, the Israel Philharmonic Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, the Montreal Symphony Orchestra, the National Symphony Orchestra, the Orchestre de Paris, the Philharmonia Orchestra, and the Vienna Philharmonic. In 1980, he performed at Royal Albert Hall for the BBC Proms. In 1982, at age 20, he was invited by President Ronald Reagan and First Lady Nancy Reagan to perform with violinist Itzhak Perlman in the East Room of the White House, the performance being recorded for the PBS television program *In Performance at the White House*. In 1983, he closed the Mostly Mozart Festival at Lincoln Center with Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 1 conducted by Leonard Slatkin. In 1989, he performed in concert with the Emerson String Quartet for the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center. In 1991, Noda ceased his performance career after becoming disillusioned with the classical musical world and the role he played in it. In a later interview with The New York Times, he stated that young people are drawn to romance, war, and good-and-evil stories because their emotional lives are largely fantasy, and that this imaginative capacity, while essential to talent, diminishes over time, leading many prodigies to experience midlife crises in their late teens or early twenties if their imagination is not replenished by experience. After halting his performance career, Noda joined the Metropolitan Opera as a vocal coach and administrator in 1991 and has since performed only rarely as a soloist. He continues to perform regularly as an accompanist to singers in recitals in New York City, having accompanied performers such as those listed. Since 1999, he has taught on the faculty at the Marlboro Music School and Festival. He has also spent four summers teaching at the Renata Scotto Opera Academy and gives master classes in opera at the Yale School of Music and the Juilliard School. He currently serves on the staff of the Metropolitan Opera as an instructor to singers in the Lindemann Young Artist Development Program and has served as a judge for the final round of the Metropolitan Opera National Council Auditions. He began working at the Met as a vocal coach in 1991.
